title: Increased interannual variability of Sahel rainfall under greenhouse warming

paper_content.abstract: The Sahel is home to tens of millions of people in developing regions and is frequently influenced by extreme events such as drought and floods. Multi-model mean projections indicate an increase in Sahel mean rainfall under greenhouse warming, but how Sahel rainfall interannual variability and extreme seasons might change is unclear. Using the latest generation of climate models, here we find that under a high emission scenario, Sahel rainfall variability increases, featuring a higher frequency of both extreme wet and dry seasons. The increase of rainfall interannual variability is stronger in the central-eastern Sahel than in the western Sahel. The increase in variability is due to several factors, including a projected increase in El Niño-Southern Oscillation variability, which leads to a stronger impact on low-level wind and moisture flux over the Sahel resulting in more extreme seasons, and a higher mean rainfall over the Sahel favoring large anomalies. Thus, the Sahel is likely to experience more extreme wet and dry seasons relative to its warmer and wetter mean climate.
paper_content.introduction:
The Sahel is located in a transition area south of the Sahara Desert and north of the wet tropical rainforests with strong interannual/seasonal rainfall variability. Both drought and flood conditions can lead to devastating impacts on local rainfed agriculture and the people dependent on it. In particular, extreme dry years superimposed on the long-term drought, as seen in 1984, can affect a large portion of the population in countries like Sudan and cause food shortages for millions of people.

Sahel rainfall is concentrated in the July-August-September (JAS) season, following the seasonal marching of the western African monsoon. Interannual (or JAS) Sahel rainfall variability is influenced by tropical sea surface temperature (SST) variability. For example, warming of the eastern Pacific during a developing El Niño event can lead to a dry Sahel by increasing the upper tropospheric temperature over the tropics and the atmospheric stability above the Sahel, and forcing easterly wind anomalies over the Sahel as a Gill-Matsuno response which transport moisture out of the Sahel. The Atlantic Niño/Niña, featuring positive (negative) SST anomalies over the equatorial Atlantic, can reduce (increase) low-level pressure gradient between North Africa and the equator and weaken (strengthen) the monsoon, leading to a dry (wet) Sahel.

The interannual relationship between tropical SST and Sahel rainfall is unstable and modulated by the background climate mean state change. While the Atlantic Niño tends to lead to dry anomalies over Sahel pre-1970s, the negative relationship between the Atlantic SST and Sahel rainfall breaks down post-1970s. Post-1970s, an Atlantic Niño event is accompanied by negative anomalies of tropical eastern Pacific SST, which offset the drying effect of the Atlantic Niño and dominate Sahel rainfall variability in recent decades. The change in the interannual tropical SST–Sahel rainfall relationship is related to the decadal background SST mean state fluctuations, which determine the location of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ; influenced by the interhemispheric SST gradients in the Atlantic Ocean) and the amplitude of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) (associated with Pacific SST mean state). The modulation of the tropical SST–Sahel rainfall linkage by the climate mean state in recent decades implies that the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall may change in response to future shifts in the mean state under global warming.

Previous studies of future changes in Sahel rainfall have primarily focused on the changes in climatological means and sub-seasonal timescales. Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6) models tend to show a wetter Sahel mean state in the 21st century compared with the 20th century under greenhouse warming, driven by mechanisms such as a faster warming in the northern hemisphere, favoring moisture convergence in the North Atlantic and the enhanced land–sea warming contrast which moves the rain band northward to the Sahel. On daily to sub-seasonal scales, greenhouse warming tends to induce more extreme rainfall days associated with mesoscale convective systems due to the strengthening of the meridional temperature gradient over the Sahel, but a reduction in the total number of rainy days.

How variability of Sahel rainfall on interannual timescales will change in a warmer and wetter mean climate under greenhouse warming is unclear. Using the latest climate models in CMIP6, here we show a robust increase in JAS Sahel rainfall variability in the 21st century under a high emission scenario, accompanied by an increase in both extreme dry and wet seasons.
paper_content.results:
Increased variability of Sahel rainfall and occurrence of extreme seasons
We use 42 available CMIP6 models forced with historical forcing from 1900 to 2014 and with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 5-8.5 high emission scenario from 2015 to 2099, and evaluate the Sahel (11°N to 15°N, 17°W to 40°E) rainfall interannual variability change, represented by the standard deviation of JAS rainfall anomalies, from the 20th century (1900–1999) to the 21st century (2000–2099) (see “Observation and CMIP6 data” in Methods).

Most of the CMIP6 models (39 out of the total 42 models, 93%) show an increase in JAS Sahel rainfall variability from the 20th century to the 21st century but with a large spread in the magnitude of change (Fig. 1a). The multi-model mean increase is statistically significant according to a bootstrap test (see “Bootstrap test” in Methods) (Fig. 1a). There is no significant relationship between model performance in simulating present-day Sahel rainfall variability and the magnitude of the projected change (see “Sensitivity test” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 1).

The increase in rainfall variability is underpinned by an increase in the frequency of extreme seasons. A majority of the models project not only more extreme wet seasons (defined as years with JAS rainfall anomalies larger than 1.5 standard deviations; 40 out of the 42 models, 95%) but also more extreme dry seasons (defined as years with JAS rainfall anomalies smaller than −1.5 standard deviations; 30 out of the 42 models, 71%) in the future, both strongly correlated with the increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Fig. 1b, c). The multi-model mean projects a 140% (60%) increase in the frequency of extreme wet (dry) seasons, from 4.4 (4.3) events per 100 years in the 20th century to 10.6 (6.9) events per 100 years in the 21st century. Using other thresholds for defining extreme seasons yields similar results (Supplementary Fig. 2). The overall wetting trend means that future dry seasons may be less severe in absolute terms, but strong negative rainfall anomalies (relative to the elevated future rainfall climatology) will pose substantial risks to local communities and ecosystems that have adapted to a wetter environment.

Previous studies have suggested that the response of rainfall over the western Sahel (17°W to 5°W) and central-eastern Sahel (CE, 5°W to 40°E) to greenhouse warming might be different (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods). Indeed, the interannual rainfall variability increase from the 20th century to the 21st century is more robust over the CE Sahel (all 42 models show an increase) than over the western Sahel (79% of the models show an increase). The increase in variability translates to more extreme dry and wet seasons in the CE Sahel and more extreme wet seasons in the western Sahel. The change of the frequency of extreme dry seasons in the western Sahel has no inter-model consensus (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods).

We also examine the change of Sahel rainfall variability under a SSP1-2.6 low emission scenario in 39 available CMIP6 models. A total of 32 out of the 39 models (82%) show an increased Sahel rainfall variability from the 20th century to the 21st century under the SSP1-2.6 emission scenario (Supplementary Fig. 3). The inter-model consensus is weaker compared to that under the SSP 5-8.5 emission scenario (93%), and the multi-model mean change of rainfall variability (0.07 mm/day) is smaller than that under the high emission scenario (0.15 mm/day). We then focus on the high emission scenario to explore the mechanisms driving the increase in Sahel rainfall variability.

A stronger influence from ENSO under greenhouse warming
We start by examining changes in the impact of tropical SST variability on the Sahel rainfall variability. As expected, the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall is dominated by the tropical eastern Pacific SST (ENSO) variability in observations from 1979 to 2022 (Supplementary Fig. 4a). A developing El Niño in JAS is associated with negative rainfall anomalies over the whole Sahel with the strongest anomalies located in the central Sahel (Supplementary Fig. 4b). The Pacific anomalous warming stimulates local convection and rearranges the atmosphere circulation in the tropics through a Gill-Matsuno like response and modulation of the Walker circulation, inducing low-level high pressure anomalies in the tropical north Atlantic and surface easterly wind anomalies over the Sahel (Supplementary Fig. 4c). The low-level easterly wind transports moisture out of the Sahel and causes negative rainfall anomalies.

Most of the CMIP6 models (36 out of 42, 86%) project an increase in JAS ENSO variability (represented by JAS Niño 3.4 index) in the 21st century and models with a stronger increase in ENSO variability systematically simulate a stronger increase in Sahel rainfall variability with a significant inter-model correlation of 0.53, scaled by the global SST warming rate (Fig. 2a). Even without stronger ENSO SST variability, greenhouse warming tends to amplify the impact of ENSO on Sahel rainfall. The amplification is associated with a faster eastern Pacific warming than the surrounding regions, which enhances local convection and increases the sensitivity of lower-tropospheric humidity to ENSO. When combined with increased ENSO variability, the overall Sahel rainfall response to ENSO becomes stronger under greenhouse warming. Consistently, most models (38 out of 42) simulate a stronger total response of Sahel rainfall to ENSO from the 20th century to the 21st century, represented by a regression of Sahel rainfall onto normalized Niño 3.4 index in each period; the stronger the increase in Sahel rainfall response to ENSO, the greater the increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Fig. 2b) (see “Sensitivity test” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 5a). The stronger impact from ENSO contributes to the increased variability of rainfall in both western Sahel and CE Sahel, while the inter-model correlation of rainfall variability changes and ENSO variability changes is higher for the CE Sahel than that for the western Sahel (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods).

In a warmer climate, a developing El Niño in JAS can lead to stronger easterly wind anomaly over the Sahel and the North Atlantic, which transports moisture out of the Sahel and inhibits rainfall (Fig. 2c), either through stronger Kelvin waves propagating eastward from the Pacific or through stronger Rossby waves generated by the convection anomalies over the Indian Ocean. The low-level wind change is also associated with a weakened monsoon, preventing the northward movement of the rain belt and drying the Sahel (Fig. 2c). A total of 37 out of 42 models project an increase in 850 hPa zonal wind variability over the Sahel; a stronger increase in zonal wind variability is systematically associated with a stronger increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Fig. 2d) (see “Sensitivity test” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 5b).

In observations, a developing El Niño event is often accompanied by an Atlantic Niño pattern in the equatorial eastern Atlantic (Supplementary Fig. 6), which typically weakens the drying effect of El Niño on Sahel rainfall by moving the ITCZ northward and strengthening the monsoon. Under greenhouse warming, Atlantic Niño/Niña variability is projected to decrease. This reduction may favor an increase in Sahel rainfall variability by diminishing the offsetting effect of Atlantic Niño/Niña on ENSO influences (see “Possible role of the reduced Atlantic Niño/Niña variability” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 7).

A wetter mean state conducive to rainfall variability
We also examine the impact of the increase in local seasonal mean rainfall. Comparing the 21st century and 20th century, models that simulate a larger increase in JAS mean rainfall tend to project a stronger increase in JAS rainfall interannual variability over the Sahel (Fig. 3a). The inter-model correlation between the mean state change and interannual variability change of JAS Sahel rainfall is 0.53, which is significant above the 95% confidence level. The relationship between changes in rainfall interannual variability and changes in local mean state is robust across 42 models for both the western Sahel and CE Sahel regions (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods).

In terms of extreme seasons, a wetter mean state contributes to more extreme dry seasons over the Sahel in the 21st century, with an inter-model correlation of 0.46 across 42 models, significant at the 95% confidence level (Fig. 3b). A weak relationship is found between rainfall mean state change and change in extreme wet seasons (Fig. 3c). An increased climatological rainfall is conducive to more extreme dry seasons relative to that climatology, because the dry mean state in the current climate may limit substantial negative rainfall anomalies, even when a strong El Niño occurs.

The projected increase of JAS Sahel mean rainfall is suggested to be related to the SST mean state change. Here we find a close relationship between the Sahel mean rainfall change and the Atlantic SST gradient change (defined as the difference in JAS SST between averages over the 0°−30°N, 60°W−17°W, and 30°S−0°, 60°W−10°E area) (Fig. 3d). A warmer north Atlantic than the south Atlantic favors a northward movement of the ITCZ and strengthens the monsoon, which promotes more rainfall over the Sahel on long timescales and induces stronger interannual variability. In the 42 CMIP6 models, the Sahel rainfall mean state change yields a weak inter-model correlation with ENSO variability change (Supplementary Fig. 8), suggesting that it contributes to the change in Sahel rainfall variability independent from that by the ENSO variability change.

In addition to the influence of SST mean pattern change, previous studies have also highlighted the roles of uniform SST warming and the direct radiative effects of increased CO₂ in driving changes in the Sahel mean rainfall. Below, we further investigate changes in the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall under the impact of uniform SST warming and direct radiative forcing, excluding the effects of changes in SST interannual variability (such as ENSO) and SST warming patterns (differential Atlantic SST warming), using simulations from Atmospheric Model Intercomparison Project (AMIP) experiments.

Opposing impact from uniform SST warming and direct radiative effect
We compare Sahel rainfall variability in the simulations of 10 models participating in the AMIP and AMIP-p4k experiments from CMIP6 (see “Analysis of AMIP experiments” in Methods) to explore the effect of uniform SST warming on Sahel rainfall variability change. The AMIP experiments are forced with observed SSTs from 1979–2013, and in the AMIP-p4k experiments, a uniform warming of 4 K is added to observed SST variability (see Supplementary Fig. 9a for an example; see “Analysis of AMIP experiments” in Methods). In these two sets of experiments, SST properties, such as ENSO and SST mean pattern, remain the same.

Greenhouse warming tends to increase rainfall variability by increasing the specific humidity of the atmosphere and boosting rainfall event even though the circulation is unchanged. However, this can be offset by the stabilization of the atmosphere that is also caused by global warming. As expected, low level (850 hPa) specific humidity is increased from the AMIP experiment to the AMIP-p4k experiment in all 10 models (Supplementary Fig. 10a). However, no significant change of JAS Sahel rainfall variability is observed in the AMIP-p4k experiments compared with the AMIP experiments, with 5 models showing an increase while the other 5 models showing a decrease (Fig. 4a). The multi-model mean change shows a decrease that is not statistically significant (Fig. 4a).

All 10 AMIP-p4k experiments show a drier Sahel mean state compared with the AMIP experiments (Supplementary Fig. 10b), which may reduce Sahel rainfall variability. Similar to the mean state–interannual variability relationship in Fig. 3a, models with a larger decrease in mean rainfall from the AMIP experiment to the AMIP-p4k experiment tend to simulate a larger decrease in Sahel rainfall variability. Thus, a uniform SST warming with unchanged SST variability is not responsible for the projected increase in Sahel rainfall variability by CMIP6 models.

The direct radiative effect of the increased CO₂ has an opposite impact on the Sahel rainfall mean state and interannual variability change to that from uniform SST warming. Here we examine the direct radiative effect using 10 AMIP-4CO₂ experiments forced with observed SSTs but with CO₂ levels multiplied by four (see “Analysis of AMIP experiments” in Methods). The direct radiative effect of increased greenhouse gas emissions, measured as the difference between the AMIP-4CO₂ and the AMIP experiments, tends to warm North Africa (see Supplementary Fig. 9b for an example) and weaken the shallow meridional circulation, as characterized by the northward near-surface flow from the Sahel to the Sahara accompanied by 700 hPa southward dry flow from the Sahara to the Sahel. The weakened dry flow from the north enhances JAS Sahel rainfall (Supplementary Fig. 10c), which in turn leads to stronger interannual variability of Sahel rainfall in AMIP-4CO₂ experiments (Fig. 4b). Thus, the uniform SST warming and direct radiative effect tend to have opposite impacts on Sahel rainfall mean state and interannual variability.
paper_content.methods:
Observation and CMIP6 data
We focus on the JAS rainfall variability change over the Sahel (17°W to 40°E, 11°N to 15°N). Monthly averaged total rainfall, SST, sea level pressure, and 850 hPa wind field data from ERA5 (fifth generation of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts atmospheric reanalyses) dataset are used as observations to explore the variability of Sahel rainfall and its relationship with tropical SST from 1979–2022. ERA5 data have a horizontal resolution of 0.25°×0.25°. All anomalies are calculated relative to the climatology from 1979 to 2022 after a quadratic detrending.

A total of 42 available CMIP6 models forced with historical forcing from 1900 to 2014 and with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 5-8.5 emission scenario from 2015 to 2099, are used to investigate changes in Sahel rainfall variability under greenhouse warming and associated mechanisms. Data of 39 models (data of the three models are unavailable) forced with SSP1-2.6 emission scenario from 2015 to 2099 are also used to explore the Sahel rainfall variability change under a low emission scenario. A total of 28 CMIP5 models forced under historical forcing to 2005 and future greenhouse gas forcing till 2099 under the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 (RCP85) are applied to examine the rainfall variability change. All the monthly rainfall, SST, and wind field data are interpolated to a 1°×1° horizontal resolution. Similar to observations, anomalies are calculated with reference to the climatology of the whole period (200 years from 1900 to 2099) after removing the quadratic trend.

We use a t-test to perform the significance test for the correlation coefficient.

The extreme dry and wet rainfall seasons in each model are defined as the years with JAS rainfall anomalies smaller (larger) than −1.5 (1.5) s.d. of the 200-year climate. The long-term trend has been removed, and the extreme seasons in the 20th century and the 21st century are defined relative to their corresponding climatology.

Bootstrap test
A bootstrap test method is used to examine the significance of multi-model mean change. As in Fig. 1a, we randomly resample the 42 values of Sahel rainfall variability in the 20th century to conduct 10,000 realizations of 42-sample Sahel rainfall variability, and any sample value can be repeated. The same analysis is repeated for the 21st century. The multi-model mean change of Sahel rainfall variability is significant at the 95% confidence level if the multi-model mean change is greater than the sum of the standard deviations of the 10,000 realizations in the two centuries. The error bars in the multi-model mean in Fig. 1a show the one standard deviation of the 10,000 realizations. The same method is used to test the significance of the changes in Sahel rainfall variability and mean state, and 850 hPa specific humidity in AMIP experiments.

Sensitivity test
We apply a quadratic detrending method for calculating the anomalies, which estimates and removes the least-squares quadratic trend from the time series, because the global warming trend is not linear. We also calculate anomalies using an 11-year running window to remove decadal-scale variability. In this method, anomalies for 1900–1904 and 2095–2099 are referenced to the climatology of 1900–1910 and 2089–2099, respectively. The remaining anomalies are obtained using an 11-year running climatology. Both methods yield similar results.

Without model selection, the majority of CMIP6 models indicate an increased Sahel rainfall variability due to greenhouse warming. We further assess the potential influence of present-day model performance on this projection using two metrics: the regional average of rainfall variability and the spatial pattern correlation of variability with observations over the Sahel. The results reveal that the ability of simulating present-day rainfall interannual variability has a negligible impact on its future change (Supplementary Fig. 1).

Changes from the 20th century to the 21st century are scaled by the global SST warming rate over the same period to limit the influence of the different climate sensitivities in models. Sahel rainfall variability change in two models is abnormally larger than in other models after scaling by the global warming rate (Fig. 2b, d). However, the scaling process has little qualitative impact on our results (see Supplementary Fig. 5 for examples).

West-east contrast
Rainfall over the western Sahel and CE Sahel tends to have different responses to greenhouse warming. While the climate models simulate increased rainfall over the CE Sahel, rainfall over the western Sahel shows less change in the 21st century under the high emission scenario. We compare the interannual rainfall variability change over the two regions.

Over the western Sahel, 33 out of the total 42 CMIP6 models (79%) show an increase in JAS rainfall variability from the 20th century to the 21st century. However, the multi-model mean change of the rainfall variability is not significant according to the bootstrap test. The increase of interannual variability translates into more extreme wet (>1.5 s.d.; 33 out of the total 42 CMIP6 models) seasons in the future over the western Sahel. The change of the frequency of the extreme dry seasons (<−1.5 s.d.) has no inter-model consensus, with 20 models showing an increase.

The interannual variability of rainfall over the CE Sahel in the 42 models all show an increase in the 21st century. The multi-model mean change is significant according to the bootstrap test. The increased variability leads to more extreme wet (40 out of the 42 models show an increase) and dry (33 out of the 42 models show an increase) seasons over the CE Sahel in the future.

The increased variability of ENSO under greenhouse warming leads to stronger rainfall variability in both the western Sahel and CE Sahel. The inter-model correlation between rainfall variability change and ENSO variability change from the 20th century to the 21st century among 42 models is 0.32 for the western Sahel and 0.5 for the CE Sahel, both significant above the 95% confidence level.

The interannual rainfall variability changes in the western Sahel and the CE Sahel under greenhouse warming are both related to the projected local rainfall mean state change. The inter-model correlation between rainfall variability change and local rainfall mean state change from the 20th century to the 21st century among 42 models is 0.47 for the western Sahel and 0.63 for the CE Sahel, both significantly above the 95% confidence level.

Possible role of the reduced Atlantic Niño/Niña variability
Under greenhouse warming, ENSO exerts a stronger impact on Sahel rainfall, while the influence from the Atlantic is weaker, a change somewhat similar to that observed since the 1970s. Models have shown that the Atlantic Niño/Niña by itself is an important source modulating Sahel rainfall. Under greenhouse warming, climate models simulate a reduction in Atlantic Niño/Niña variability. Models with a larger decrease in the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability (represented by the standard deviation of SST anomalies averaged over 3°S to 3°N, 20°W to 0°E) tend to simulate a greater increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Supplementary Fig. 7a).

However, we do not find a statistically significant inter-model correlation between Sahel rainfall variability and the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability in the simulated present-day climate. One possible reason for a future reduction in Atlantic Niño/Niña variability to favor an increase in Sahel rainfall variability might be that the offsetting effect of the Atlantic Niño/Niña on ENSO–Sahel rainfall connection is weaker when the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability decreases. For example, an El Niño event is often accompanied with negative SST anomalies over the equatorial eastern Atlantic, that is, an Atlantic Niña condition (Supplementary Fig. 6). Cool tropical Atlantic SSTs promote stronger temperature gradients between the tropical Atlantic and Sahara, strengthening the monsoon and pushing the ITCZ northward, favoring Sahel rainfall and offsetting the drying effect of the El Niño. In a warmer climate, reduced Atlantic Niño/Niña variability limits the offsetting effect. Compared with the 20th century, the response of the ITCZ to an Atlantic Niña is much weaker in the 21st century, featuring a southward retreat resembling its response to El Niño (comparing Supplementary Fig. 7b and Fig. 2c). In this case, an El Niño moves the ITCZ and the rainfall belt over the North Atlantic southward more easily and induces a dry condition over the Sahel. In addition, the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability change shows a weak relationship with the ENSO variability change and the Sahel rainfall mean state change (Supplementary Fig. 13), suggesting their independent roles.

Analysis of AMIP experiments
AMIP, AMIP-p4k and AMIP-4CO₂ experiments from 10 available CMIP6 models from 1979 to 2013 are used to explore the effect of greenhouse warming on Sahel rainfall variability with fixed SST variability. Monthly data are interpolated to a 1°×1° horizontal resolution. Anomalies are calculated with reference to the climatology of 1979 to 2013 after removing the quadratic trend.

AMIP experiments are based on atmospheric models forced by observed SST and sea ice concentrations. AMIP-p4k experiments have similar settings to AMIP experiments except that a uniform 4 K warming is added to the SST (see Supplementary Fig. 9a for an example). AMIP-4CO₂ experiments are forced with observed SSTs but with CO₂ levels multiplied by four (see Supplementary Fig. 9b for an example). Thus, the SST mean state pattern and SST interannual variability are the same between the three sets of experiments. The difference between AMIP and AMIP-p4k experiments can represent the influence of the uniform SST warming, and the difference between AMIP and AMIP-4CO₂ experiments can represent the influence of the direct radiative effect of CO₂.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Review comments/suggestions on the manuscript entitled "Increased interannual variability of Sahel rainfall under greenhouse warming"
Summary
The Sahel is one of the regions in the developing world that is particularly susceptible to the effects of climate change. The
impacts of climate change are most evident in rainfall, which has become increasingly variable in recent years. The increase
in interannual variability of rainfall is associated with an increased frequency of extreme events such as droughts and floods.
This has devastating impacts on the millions of people who rely on rain-fed agriculture as their main economic activity for
sustaining their livelihoods through income and food. To alleviate these impacts and safeguard the security and
sustainability of economic and social development, it is crucial to understand the future changes in interannual rainfall
variability over the Sahel region. The authors projected an increased interannual variability of rainfall contributed by both wet
and dry extreme seasonal events, with contrasting magnitude between central-eastern and western Sahel. Finally, they
discussed the possible mechanism for such an increase in interannual rainfall variability, as derived from ENSO and mean
rainfall.
The work is comprehensive and has potential interests, especially in a region where the performance evaluation of the
models and prediction has been challenging. The manuscript has clear content and is well organized. It has the qualities
that align with the theme and weight of the journal. As such, it is commendable. But there are a couple of issues that need to
be addressed before further consideration, as detailed hereunder.
Major concerns:
1. The main focus is the changes in interannual variability of rainfall. However, Sahel rainfall also exhibits decadal and
interdecadal components, as exemplified by the shift from a wet state in the 1950s and 1960s to a dry state in the 1970s and
1980s.The likes of these changes might appear in future periods [e.g. Dieppois et al. (2013); García-Serrano et al. (2013)].
How did the authors deal with the decadal signals in the Sahel rainfall?
References
Dieppois, Bastien, Arona Diedhiou, Alain Durand, Matthieu Fournier, Nicolas Massei, David Sebag, Yongkang Xue, and
Bernard Fontaine. 2013. “Quasi-Decadal Signals of Sahel Rainfall and West African Monsoon since the Mid-Twentieth
Century.” Journal of Geophysical Research Atmospheres 118(22): 12,587-12,599.
García-Serrano, J., F. J. Doblas-Reyes, R. J. Haarsma, and I. Polo. 2013. “Decadal Prediction of the Dominant West African
Monsoon Rainfall Modes.” Journal of Geophysical Research Atmospheres 118(11): 5260–79.
2. The authors used 42 models for computing future changes in interannual variability of rainfall. What were the selection
criteria for the models? How about evaluating model performance to simulate rainfall interannual variability relative to
observation data in the historical period, then consider only best-performing models for future changes? Although this is not
the central idea of the work, it is an important preparatory step for addressing the main idea of this work. These kinds of
analyses can be added to the supplementary information.
3. Although the discussion of the results is satisfactory, it can be further improved by highlighting some insights from the
previous generation of CMIP models. If there is related work concerning simulating the interannual rainfall variability based
on previous model versions, In the discussion, the authors should consider comparing their findings with those of related
studies (say "CMIP5 and 6") over the study region and beyond and most importantly, give the possible
implications/applications of the findings on climate/agriculture/environment etc.
Minor issues:
1. P2, L23: I am a bit confused with the use of the word "countries". I was expecting to see the word "regions" because the
sentence begin with "The Sahel…". Kindly check it.
2. P2, L32: Remove the acronym "ENSO" because it has not been used elsewhere in the abstract.
3. P3, L38: I don't see the need to put the word "dry" before "Sahara Desert" because it is known that the desert is a dry area.
Consider removing it.
4. L64, P3: Kindly provide the abbreviation for "ENSO" on its first appearance in the main text section.
5. P4, L88: Add a space between degree and lat/lon direction. Check it throughout the manuscript and for other cases of
similar concern.
6. P4, L89-90: I am wondering why the change in standard deviation rainfall was taken between 2000-2099 and 1900-1999
and not between 2015-2099 and 1900-2014? The historical period in which models are forced by historical forcings ends in
2014, and afterward, the models are forced by SSP scenarios.
7. P4, L91: What is quadratic detrend? What's its strength over common linear detrend methods in the context of rainfall?
The authors can briefly describe it in the methods section. Moreover, this last line (L90-93) describing quadratic trends may
not be necessary here because it is basically the repetition of what has been described in the methods section.
8. Fig. 1a: In the caption, the authors mentioned that green circles denote the models that feature a decrease in precipitation
variability. But, looking at the MCM-UA-1-0 model, it shows no change in std values between the two periods. Kindly check
it.
9. Extended Data Fig. 2a: There is a white line at around zero longitude. The authors can sort out the issue.
10. Extended Data Fig. 2: Which method did you use to perform the significance test for the correlations? Is a significance
test also performed on the wind pattern? The authors can briefly introduce the method in the methods section.
11. P7, L172: Is it a double hyphen?
12. P7, L180-183: A bit hard to follow this sentence. Consider revising it to enhance understanding.
13. Fig. 4a: The std values of HadGEM3-GC31-ALL between AMIP and AMIP-p4k simulations are comparable, and yet the
model is incorporated in the group of models showing increasing tendency. Could you clarify this?
14. Fig. 4a: In the first line of the caption, 1979 to 2013? Did you mean 1979 to 2023? Also, in the fourth line from the end of
the caption concerning the green circles, did you mean a decrease or an increase?
15. P19, L 466: Adjust spacing before JAS
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Review of
“Increased interannual variability of Sahel rainfall under greenhouse warming”
This paper highlights the increase in interannual variability in rainfall over the Sahel, and links this increase to changes in
ENSO, the mean state and changes in the Atlantic SSTs. It also shows that uniform SST changes and radiative changes
due to increased carbon dioxide levels have opposite effects on rainfall variability over the Sahel.
The paper is robust and interesting, and is an important contribution to the literature. I recommend minor revisions.
Major-minor comments:
I think the section at the beginning of the discussion and conclusions on the role of the Atlantic should be a separate section
in the results. The discussion and conclusions I feel should not introduce new results, which this section does.
The conclusion that there are more extreme dry seasons is based on the mean rainfall increasing, and therefore there being

Major concerns:

rainfall also exhibits decadal and interdecadal components, as exemplified by the shift
from a wet state in the 1950s and 1960s to a dry state in the 1970s and 1980s.The likes
of these changes might appear in future periods [e.g. Dieppois et al. (2013); García-
Serrano et al. (2013)]. How did the authors deal with the decadal signals in the Sahel
rainfall?
References
Dieppois, Bastien, Arona Diedhiou, Alain Durand, Matthieu Fournier, Nicolas Massei,
David Sebag, Yongkang Xue, and Bernard Fontaine. 2013. “Quasi-Decadal Signals of
Sahel Rainfall and West African Monsoon since the Mid-Twentieth Century.” Journal
of Geophysical Research Atmospheres 118(22): 12,587-12,599.
García-Serrano, J., F. J. Doblas-Reyes, R. J. Haarsma, and I. Polo. 2013. “Decadal
Prediction of the Dominant West African Monsoon Rainfall Modes.” Journal of

the provided references to the manuscript. While we acknowledge the importance of
this low-frequency signal, the primary focus of our work is on projecting future changes
in interannual rainfall variability, above changes in the mean state.
In the original version, we detrended the data and compared the changes between two
100-year periods. This approach minimizes the influence of low-frequency decadal
variability while emphasizing the long-term greenhouse warming signal.
To test the robustness of our results, we have implemented an additional method to
remove decadal influence. This method calculates SST anomalies using an evolving
climatology: a 11-year running window is used for the core period (e.g., the anomaly
for the year 2000 is referenced to the 1995–2005 mean); the anomalies during the 1900-
1904 and 2095-2099 are calculated relative to the fixed climatology of 1900-1910 and
2089-2099, respectively.

nearly identical to our original method (Fig. R1). The inter-model correlation of the
projected change in Sahel rainfall interannual variability between the two methods is

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The Sahel is home to tens of millions of people in developing regions and is frequently influenced by extreme events such as drought and floods. Multi-model mean projections indicate an increase in Sahel mean rainfall under greenhouse warming, but how Sahel rainfall interannual variability and extreme seasons might change is unclear. Using the latest generation of climate models, here we find that under a high emission scenario, Sahel rainfall variability increases, featuring a higher frequency of both extreme wet and dry seasons. The increase of rainfall interannual variability is stronger in the central-eastern Sahel than in the western Sahel. The increase in variability is due to several factors, including a projected increase in El Niño-Southern Oscillation variability, which leads to a stronger impact on low-level wind and moisture flux over the Sahel resulting in more extreme seasons, and a higher mean rainfall over the Sahel favoring large anomalies. Thus, the Sahel is likely to experience more extreme wet and dry seasons relative to its warmer and wetter mean climate.

---

## Introduction

The Sahel is located in a transition area south of the Sahara Desert and north of the wet tropical rainforests with strong interannual/seasonal rainfall variability. Both drought and flood conditions can lead to devastating impacts on local rainfed agriculture and the people dependent on it. In particular, extreme dry years superimposed on the long-term drought, as seen in 1984, can affect a large portion of the population in countries like Sudan and cause food shortages for millions of people.

Sahel rainfall is concentrated in the July-August-September (JAS) season, following the seasonal marching of the western African monsoon. Interannual (or JAS) Sahel rainfall variability is influenced by tropical sea surface temperature (SST) variability. For example, warming of the eastern Pacific during a developing El Niño event can lead to a dry Sahel by increasing the upper tropospheric temperature over the tropics and the atmospheric stability above the Sahel, and forcing easterly wind anomalies over the Sahel as a Gill-Matsuno response which transport moisture out of the Sahel. The Atlantic Niño/Niña, featuring positive (negative) SST anomalies over the equatorial Atlantic, can reduce (increase) low-level pressure gradient between North Africa and the equator and weaken (strengthen) the monsoon, leading to a dry (wet) Sahel.

The interannual relationship between tropical SST and Sahel rainfall is unstable and modulated by the background climate mean state change. While the Atlantic Niño tends to lead to dry anomalies over Sahel pre-1970s, the negative relationship between the Atlantic SST and Sahel rainfall breaks down post-1970s. Post-1970s, an Atlantic Niño event is accompanied by negative anomalies of tropical eastern Pacific SST, which offset the drying effect of the Atlantic Niño and dominate Sahel rainfall variability in recent decades. The change in the interannual tropical SST–Sahel rainfall relationship is related to the decadal background SST mean state fluctuations, which determine the location of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ; influenced by the interhemispheric SST gradients in the Atlantic Ocean) and the amplitude of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) (associated with Pacific SST mean state). The modulation of the tropical SST–Sahel rainfall linkage by the climate mean state in recent decades implies that the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall may change in response to future shifts in the mean state under global warming.

Previous studies of future changes in Sahel rainfall have primarily focused on the changes in climatological means and sub-seasonal timescales. Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6) models tend to show a wetter Sahel mean state in the 21st century compared with the 20th century under greenhouse warming, driven by mechanisms such as a faster warming in the northern hemisphere, favoring moisture convergence in the North Atlantic and the enhanced land–sea warming contrast which moves the rain band northward to the Sahel. On daily to sub-seasonal scales, greenhouse warming tends to induce more extreme rainfall days associated with mesoscale convective systems due to the strengthening of the meridional temperature gradient over the Sahel, but a reduction in the total number of rainy days.

How variability of Sahel rainfall on interannual timescales will change in a warmer and wetter mean climate under greenhouse warming is unclear. Using the latest climate models in CMIP6, here we show a robust increase in JAS Sahel rainfall variability in the 21st century under a high emission scenario, accompanied by an increase in both extreme dry and wet seasons.

---

## Results

Increased variability of Sahel rainfall and occurrence of extreme seasons
We use 42 available CMIP6 models forced with historical forcing from 1900 to 2014 and with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 5-8.5 high emission scenario from 2015 to 2099, and evaluate the Sahel (11°N to 15°N, 17°W to 40°E) rainfall interannual variability change, represented by the standard deviation of JAS rainfall anomalies, from the 20th century (1900–1999) to the 21st century (2000–2099) (see “Observation and CMIP6 data” in Methods).

Most of the CMIP6 models (39 out of the total 42 models, 93%) show an increase in JAS Sahel rainfall variability from the 20th century to the 21st century but with a large spread in the magnitude of change (Fig. 1a). The multi-model mean increase is statistically significant according to a bootstrap test (see “Bootstrap test” in Methods) (Fig. 1a). There is no significant relationship between model performance in simulating present-day Sahel rainfall variability and the magnitude of the projected change (see “Sensitivity test” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 1).

The increase in rainfall variability is underpinned by an increase in the frequency of extreme seasons. A majority of the models project not only more extreme wet seasons (defined as years with JAS rainfall anomalies larger than 1.5 standard deviations; 40 out of the 42 models, 95%) but also more extreme dry seasons (defined as years with JAS rainfall anomalies smaller than −1.5 standard deviations; 30 out of the 42 models, 71%) in the future, both strongly correlated with the increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Fig. 1b, c). The multi-model mean projects a 140% (60%) increase in the frequency of extreme wet (dry) seasons, from 4.4 (4.3) events per 100 years in the 20th century to 10.6 (6.9) events per 100 years in the 21st century. Using other thresholds for defining extreme seasons yields similar results (Supplementary Fig. 2). The overall wetting trend means that future dry seasons may be less severe in absolute terms, but strong negative rainfall anomalies (relative to the elevated future rainfall climatology) will pose substantial risks to local communities and ecosystems that have adapted to a wetter environment.

Previous studies have suggested that the response of rainfall over the western Sahel (17°W to 5°W) and central-eastern Sahel (CE, 5°W to 40°E) to greenhouse warming might be different (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods). Indeed, the interannual rainfall variability increase from the 20th century to the 21st century is more robust over the CE Sahel (all 42 models show an increase) than over the western Sahel (79% of the models show an increase). The increase in variability translates to more extreme dry and wet seasons in the CE Sahel and more extreme wet seasons in the western Sahel. The change of the frequency of extreme dry seasons in the western Sahel has no inter-model consensus (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods).

We also examine the change of Sahel rainfall variability under a SSP1-2.6 low emission scenario in 39 available CMIP6 models. A total of 32 out of the 39 models (82%) show an increased Sahel rainfall variability from the 20th century to the 21st century under the SSP1-2.6 emission scenario (Supplementary Fig. 3). The inter-model consensus is weaker compared to that under the SSP 5-8.5 emission scenario (93%), and the multi-model mean change of rainfall variability (0.07 mm/day) is smaller than that under the high emission scenario (0.15 mm/day). We then focus on the high emission scenario to explore the mechanisms driving the increase in Sahel rainfall variability.

A stronger influence from ENSO under greenhouse warming
We start by examining changes in the impact of tropical SST variability on the Sahel rainfall variability. As expected, the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall is dominated by the tropical eastern Pacific SST (ENSO) variability in observations from 1979 to 2022 (Supplementary Fig. 4a). A developing El Niño in JAS is associated with negative rainfall anomalies over the whole Sahel with the strongest anomalies located in the central Sahel (Supplementary Fig. 4b). The Pacific anomalous warming stimulates local convection and rearranges the atmosphere circulation in the tropics through a Gill-Matsuno like response and modulation of the Walker circulation, inducing low-level high pressure anomalies in the tropical north Atlantic and surface easterly wind anomalies over the Sahel (Supplementary Fig. 4c). The low-level easterly wind transports moisture out of the Sahel and causes negative rainfall anomalies.

Most of the CMIP6 models (36 out of 42, 86%) project an increase in JAS ENSO variability (represented by JAS Niño 3.4 index) in the 21st century and models with a stronger increase in ENSO variability systematically simulate a stronger increase in Sahel rainfall variability with a significant inter-model correlation of 0.53, scaled by the global SST warming rate (Fig. 2a). Even without stronger ENSO SST variability, greenhouse warming tends to amplify the impact of ENSO on Sahel rainfall. The amplification is associated with a faster eastern Pacific warming than the surrounding regions, which enhances local convection and increases the sensitivity of lower-tropospheric humidity to ENSO. When combined with increased ENSO variability, the overall Sahel rainfall response to ENSO becomes stronger under greenhouse warming. Consistently, most models (38 out of 42) simulate a stronger total response of Sahel rainfall to ENSO from the 20th century to the 21st century, represented by a regression of Sahel rainfall onto normalized Niño 3.4 index in each period; the stronger the increase in Sahel rainfall response to ENSO, the greater the increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Fig. 2b) (see “Sensitivity test” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 5a). The stronger impact from ENSO contributes to the increased variability of rainfall in both western Sahel and CE Sahel, while the inter-model correlation of rainfall variability changes and ENSO variability changes is higher for the CE Sahel than that for the western Sahel (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods).

In a warmer climate, a developing El Niño in JAS can lead to stronger easterly wind anomaly over the Sahel and the North Atlantic, which transports moisture out of the Sahel and inhibits rainfall (Fig. 2c), either through stronger Kelvin waves propagating eastward from the Pacific or through stronger Rossby waves generated by the convection anomalies over the Indian Ocean. The low-level wind change is also associated with a weakened monsoon, preventing the northward movement of the rain belt and drying the Sahel (Fig. 2c). A total of 37 out of 42 models project an increase in 850 hPa zonal wind variability over the Sahel; a stronger increase in zonal wind variability is systematically associated with a stronger increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Fig. 2d) (see “Sensitivity test” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 5b).

In observations, a developing El Niño event is often accompanied by an Atlantic Niño pattern in the equatorial eastern Atlantic (Supplementary Fig. 6), which typically weakens the drying effect of El Niño on Sahel rainfall by moving the ITCZ northward and strengthening the monsoon. Under greenhouse warming, Atlantic Niño/Niña variability is projected to decrease. This reduction may favor an increase in Sahel rainfall variability by diminishing the offsetting effect of Atlantic Niño/Niña on ENSO influences (see “Possible role of the reduced Atlantic Niño/Niña variability” in Methods; Supplementary Fig. 7).

A wetter mean state conducive to rainfall variability
We also examine the impact of the increase in local seasonal mean rainfall. Comparing the 21st century and 20th century, models that simulate a larger increase in JAS mean rainfall tend to project a stronger increase in JAS rainfall interannual variability over the Sahel (Fig. 3a). The inter-model correlation between the mean state change and interannual variability change of JAS Sahel rainfall is 0.53, which is significant above the 95% confidence level. The relationship between changes in rainfall interannual variability and changes in local mean state is robust across 42 models for both the western Sahel and CE Sahel regions (see “West-East Contrast” in Methods).

In terms of extreme seasons, a wetter mean state contributes to more extreme dry seasons over the Sahel in the 21st century, with an inter-model correlation of 0.46 across 42 models, significant at the 95% confidence level (Fig. 3b). A weak relationship is found between rainfall mean state change and change in extreme wet seasons (Fig. 3c). An increased climatological rainfall is conducive to more extreme dry seasons relative to that climatology, because the dry mean state in the current climate may limit substantial negative rainfall anomalies, even when a strong El Niño occurs.

The projected increase of JAS Sahel mean rainfall is suggested to be related to the SST mean state change. Here we find a close relationship between the Sahel mean rainfall change and the Atlantic SST gradient change (defined as the difference in JAS SST between averages over the 0°−30°N, 60°W−17°W, and 30°S−0°, 60°W−10°E area) (Fig. 3d). A warmer north Atlantic than the south Atlantic favors a northward movement of the ITCZ and strengthens the monsoon, which promotes more rainfall over the Sahel on long timescales and induces stronger interannual variability. In the 42 CMIP6 models, the Sahel rainfall mean state change yields a weak inter-model correlation with ENSO variability change (Supplementary Fig. 8), suggesting that it contributes to the change in Sahel rainfall variability independent from that by the ENSO variability change.

In addition to the influence of SST mean pattern change, previous studies have also highlighted the roles of uniform SST warming and the direct radiative effects of increased CO₂ in driving changes in the Sahel mean rainfall. Below, we further investigate changes in the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall under the impact of uniform SST warming and direct radiative forcing, excluding the effects of changes in SST interannual variability (such as ENSO) and SST warming patterns (differential Atlantic SST warming), using simulations from Atmospheric Model Intercomparison Project (AMIP) experiments.

Opposing impact from uniform SST warming and direct radiative effect
We compare Sahel rainfall variability in the simulations of 10 models participating in the AMIP and AMIP-p4k experiments from CMIP6 (see “Analysis of AMIP experiments” in Methods) to explore the effect of uniform SST warming on Sahel rainfall variability change. The AMIP experiments are forced with observed SSTs from 1979–2013, and in the AMIP-p4k experiments, a uniform warming of 4 K is added to observed SST variability (see Supplementary Fig. 9a for an example; see “Analysis of AMIP experiments” in Methods). In these two sets of experiments, SST properties, such as ENSO and SST mean pattern, remain the same.

Greenhouse warming tends to increase rainfall variability by increasing the specific humidity of the atmosphere and boosting rainfall event even though the circulation is unchanged. However, this can be offset by the stabilization of the atmosphere that is also caused by global warming. As expected, low level (850 hPa) specific humidity is increased from the AMIP experiment to the AMIP-p4k experiment in all 10 models (Supplementary Fig. 10a). However, no significant change of JAS Sahel rainfall variability is observed in the AMIP-p4k experiments compared with the AMIP experiments, with 5 models showing an increase while the other 5 models showing a decrease (Fig. 4a). The multi-model mean change shows a decrease that is not statistically significant (Fig. 4a).

All 10 AMIP-p4k experiments show a drier Sahel mean state compared with the AMIP experiments (Supplementary Fig. 10b), which may reduce Sahel rainfall variability. Similar to the mean state–interannual variability relationship in Fig. 3a, models with a larger decrease in mean rainfall from the AMIP experiment to the AMIP-p4k experiment tend to simulate a larger decrease in Sahel rainfall variability. Thus, a uniform SST warming with unchanged SST variability is not responsible for the projected increase in Sahel rainfall variability by CMIP6 models.

The direct radiative effect of the increased CO₂ has an opposite impact on the Sahel rainfall mean state and interannual variability change to that from uniform SST warming. Here we examine the direct radiative effect using 10 AMIP-4CO₂ experiments forced with observed SSTs but with CO₂ levels multiplied by four (see “Analysis of AMIP experiments” in Methods). The direct radiative effect of increased greenhouse gas emissions, measured as the difference between the AMIP-4CO₂ and the AMIP experiments, tends to warm North Africa (see Supplementary Fig. 9b for an example) and weaken the shallow meridional circulation, as characterized by the northward near-surface flow from the Sahel to the Sahara accompanied by 700 hPa southward dry flow from the Sahara to the Sahel. The weakened dry flow from the north enhances JAS Sahel rainfall (Supplementary Fig. 10c), which in turn leads to stronger interannual variability of Sahel rainfall in AMIP-4CO₂ experiments (Fig. 4b). Thus, the uniform SST warming and direct radiative effect tend to have opposite impacts on Sahel rainfall mean state and interannual variability.

---

## Methods

Observation and CMIP6 data
We focus on the JAS rainfall variability change over the Sahel (17°W to 40°E, 11°N to 15°N). Monthly averaged total rainfall, SST, sea level pressure, and 850 hPa wind field data from ERA5 (fifth generation of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts atmospheric reanalyses) dataset are used as observations to explore the variability of Sahel rainfall and its relationship with tropical SST from 1979–2022. ERA5 data have a horizontal resolution of 0.25°×0.25°. All anomalies are calculated relative to the climatology from 1979 to 2022 after a quadratic detrending.

A total of 42 available CMIP6 models forced with historical forcing from 1900 to 2014 and with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) 5-8.5 emission scenario from 2015 to 2099, are used to investigate changes in Sahel rainfall variability under greenhouse warming and associated mechanisms. Data of 39 models (data of the three models are unavailable) forced with SSP1-2.6 emission scenario from 2015 to 2099 are also used to explore the Sahel rainfall variability change under a low emission scenario. A total of 28 CMIP5 models forced under historical forcing to 2005 and future greenhouse gas forcing till 2099 under the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 (RCP85) are applied to examine the rainfall variability change. All the monthly rainfall, SST, and wind field data are interpolated to a 1°×1° horizontal resolution. Similar to observations, anomalies are calculated with reference to the climatology of the whole period (200 years from 1900 to 2099) after removing the quadratic trend.

We use a t-test to perform the significance test for the correlation coefficient.

The extreme dry and wet rainfall seasons in each model are defined as the years with JAS rainfall anomalies smaller (larger) than −1.5 (1.5) s.d. of the 200-year climate. The long-term trend has been removed, and the extreme seasons in the 20th century and the 21st century are defined relative to their corresponding climatology.

Bootstrap test
A bootstrap test method is used to examine the significance of multi-model mean change. As in Fig. 1a, we randomly resample the 42 values of Sahel rainfall variability in the 20th century to conduct 10,000 realizations of 42-sample Sahel rainfall variability, and any sample value can be repeated. The same analysis is repeated for the 21st century. The multi-model mean change of Sahel rainfall variability is significant at the 95% confidence level if the multi-model mean change is greater than the sum of the standard deviations of the 10,000 realizations in the two centuries. The error bars in the multi-model mean in Fig. 1a show the one standard deviation of the 10,000 realizations. The same method is used to test the significance of the changes in Sahel rainfall variability and mean state, and 850 hPa specific humidity in AMIP experiments.

Sensitivity test
We apply a quadratic detrending method for calculating the anomalies, which estimates and removes the least-squares quadratic trend from the time series, because the global warming trend is not linear. We also calculate anomalies using an 11-year running window to remove decadal-scale variability. In this method, anomalies for 1900–1904 and 2095–2099 are referenced to the climatology of 1900–1910 and 2089–2099, respectively. The remaining anomalies are obtained using an 11-year running climatology. Both methods yield similar results.

Without model selection, the majority of CMIP6 models indicate an increased Sahel rainfall variability due to greenhouse warming. We further assess the potential influence of present-day model performance on this projection using two metrics: the regional average of rainfall variability and the spatial pattern correlation of variability with observations over the Sahel. The results reveal that the ability of simulating present-day rainfall interannual variability has a negligible impact on its future change (Supplementary Fig. 1).

Changes from the 20th century to the 21st century are scaled by the global SST warming rate over the same period to limit the influence of the different climate sensitivities in models. Sahel rainfall variability change in two models is abnormally larger than in other models after scaling by the global warming rate (Fig. 2b, d). However, the scaling process has little qualitative impact on our results (see Supplementary Fig. 5 for examples).

West-east contrast
Rainfall over the western Sahel and CE Sahel tends to have different responses to greenhouse warming. While the climate models simulate increased rainfall over the CE Sahel, rainfall over the western Sahel shows less change in the 21st century under the high emission scenario. We compare the interannual rainfall variability change over the two regions.

Over the western Sahel, 33 out of the total 42 CMIP6 models (79%) show an increase in JAS rainfall variability from the 20th century to the 21st century. However, the multi-model mean change of the rainfall variability is not significant according to the bootstrap test. The increase of interannual variability translates into more extreme wet (>1.5 s.d.; 33 out of the total 42 CMIP6 models) seasons in the future over the western Sahel. The change of the frequency of the extreme dry seasons (<−1.5 s.d.) has no inter-model consensus, with 20 models showing an increase.

The interannual variability of rainfall over the CE Sahel in the 42 models all show an increase in the 21st century. The multi-model mean change is significant according to the bootstrap test. The increased variability leads to more extreme wet (40 out of the 42 models show an increase) and dry (33 out of the 42 models show an increase) seasons over the CE Sahel in the future.

The increased variability of ENSO under greenhouse warming leads to stronger rainfall variability in both the western Sahel and CE Sahel. The inter-model correlation between rainfall variability change and ENSO variability change from the 20th century to the 21st century among 42 models is 0.32 for the western Sahel and 0.5 for the CE Sahel, both significant above the 95% confidence level.

The interannual rainfall variability changes in the western Sahel and the CE Sahel under greenhouse warming are both related to the projected local rainfall mean state change. The inter-model correlation between rainfall variability change and local rainfall mean state change from the 20th century to the 21st century among 42 models is 0.47 for the western Sahel and 0.63 for the CE Sahel, both significantly above the 95% confidence level.

Possible role of the reduced Atlantic Niño/Niña variability
Under greenhouse warming, ENSO exerts a stronger impact on Sahel rainfall, while the influence from the Atlantic is weaker, a change somewhat similar to that observed since the 1970s. Models have shown that the Atlantic Niño/Niña by itself is an important source modulating Sahel rainfall. Under greenhouse warming, climate models simulate a reduction in Atlantic Niño/Niña variability. Models with a larger decrease in the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability (represented by the standard deviation of SST anomalies averaged over 3°S to 3°N, 20°W to 0°E) tend to simulate a greater increase in Sahel rainfall variability (Supplementary Fig. 7a).

However, we do not find a statistically significant inter-model correlation between Sahel rainfall variability and the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability in the simulated present-day climate. One possible reason for a future reduction in Atlantic Niño/Niña variability to favor an increase in Sahel rainfall variability might be that the offsetting effect of the Atlantic Niño/Niña on ENSO–Sahel rainfall connection is weaker when the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability decreases. For example, an El Niño event is often accompanied with negative SST anomalies over the equatorial eastern Atlantic, that is, an Atlantic Niña condition (Supplementary Fig. 6). Cool tropical Atlantic SSTs promote stronger temperature gradients between the tropical Atlantic and Sahara, strengthening the monsoon and pushing the ITCZ northward, favoring Sahel rainfall and offsetting the drying effect of the El Niño. In a warmer climate, reduced Atlantic Niño/Niña variability limits the offsetting effect. Compared with the 20th century, the response of the ITCZ to an Atlantic Niña is much weaker in the 21st century, featuring a southward retreat resembling its response to El Niño (comparing Supplementary Fig. 7b and Fig. 2c). In this case, an El Niño moves the ITCZ and the rainfall belt over the North Atlantic southward more easily and induces a dry condition over the Sahel. In addition, the Atlantic Niño/Niña variability change shows a weak relationship with the ENSO variability change and the Sahel rainfall mean state change (Supplementary Fig. 13), suggesting their independent roles.

Analysis of AMIP experiments
AMIP, AMIP-p4k and AMIP-4CO₂ experiments from 10 available CMIP6 models from 1979 to 2013 are used to explore the effect of greenhouse warming on Sahel rainfall variability with fixed SST variability. Monthly data are interpolated to a 1°×1° horizontal resolution. Anomalies are calculated with reference to the climatology of 1979 to 2013 after removing the quadratic trend.

AMIP experiments are based on atmospheric models forced by observed SST and sea ice concentrations. AMIP-p4k experiments have similar settings to AMIP experiments except that a uniform 4 K warming is added to the SST (see Supplementary Fig. 9a for an example). AMIP-4CO₂ experiments are forced with observed SSTs but with CO₂ levels multiplied by four (see Supplementary Fig. 9b for an example). Thus, the SST mean state pattern and SST interannual variability are the same between the three sets of experiments. The difference between AMIP and AMIP-p4k experiments can represent the influence of the uniform SST warming, and the difference between AMIP and AMIP-4CO₂ experiments can represent the influence of the direct radiative effect of CO₂.

## Paper

## Abstract

The Sahel is home to tens of millions of people in developing regions and is frequently influenced by extreme events such as drought and floods. Multi-model mean projections indicate an increase in Sahel mean rainfall under greenhouse warming, but how Sahel rainfall interannual variability and extreme seasons might change is unclear. Using the latest generation of climate models, here we find that under a high emission scenario, Sahel rainfall variability increases, featuring a higher frequency of both extreme wet and dry seasons. The increase of rainfall interannual variability is stronger in the central-eastern Sahel than in the western Sahel. The increase in variability is due to several factors, including a projected increase in El Niño-Southern Oscillation variability, which leads to a stronger impact on low-level wind and moisture flux over the Sahel resulting in more extreme seasons, and a higher mean rainfall over the Sahel favoring large anomalies. Thus, the Sahel is likely to experience more extreme wet and dry seasons relative to its warmer and wetter mean climate.

## Introduction

The Sahel is located in a transition area south of the Sahara Desert and north of the wet tropical rainforests with strong interannual/seasonal rainfall variability. Both drought and flood conditions can lead to devastating impacts on local rainfed agriculture and the people dependent on it. In particular, extreme dry years superimposed on the long-term drought, as seen in 1984, can affect a large portion of the population in countries like Sudan and cause food shortages for millions of people.

Sahel rainfall is concentrated in the July-August-September (JAS) season, following the seasonal marching of the western African monsoon. Interannual (or JAS) Sahel rainfall variability is influenced by tropical sea surface temperature (SST) variability. For example, warming of the eastern Pacific during a developing El Niño event can lead to a dry Sahel by increasing the upper tropospheric temperature over the tropics and the atmospheric stability above the Sahel, and forcing easterly wind anomalies over the Sahel as a Gill-Matsuno response which transport moisture out of the Sahel. The Atlantic Niño/Niña, featuring positive (negative) SST anomalies over the equatorial Atlantic, can reduce (increase) low-level pressure gradient between North Africa and the equator and weaken (strengthen) the monsoon, leading to a dry (wet) Sahel.

The interannual relationship between tropical SST and Sahel rainfall is unstable and modulated by the background climate mean state change. While the Atlantic Niño tends to lead to dry anomalies over Sahel pre-1970s, the negative relationship between the Atlantic SST and Sahel rainfall breaks down post-1970s. Post-1970s, an Atlantic Niño event is accompanied by negative anomalies of tropical eastern Pacific SST, which offset the drying effect of the Atlantic Niño and dominate Sahel rainfall variability in recent decades. The change in the interannual tropical SST–Sahel rainfall relationship is related to the decadal background SST mean state fluctuations, which determine the location of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ; influenced by the interhemispheric SST gradients in the Atlantic Ocean) and the amplitude of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) (associated with Pacific SST mean state). The modulation of the tropical SST–Sahel rainfall linkage by the climate mean state in recent decades implies that the interannual variability of Sahel rainfall may change in response to future shifts in the mean state under global warming.

Previous studies of future changes in Sahel rainfall have primarily focused on the changes in climatological means and sub-seasonal timescales. Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6) models tend to show a wetter Sahel mean state in the 21st century compared with the 20th century under greenhouse warming, driven by mechanisms such as a faster warming in the northern hemisphere, favoring moisture convergence in the North Atlantic and the enhanced land–sea warming contrast which moves the rain band northward to the Sahel. On daily to sub-seasonal scales, greenhouse warming tends to induce more extreme rainfall days associated with mesoscale convective systems due to the strengthening of the meridional temperature gradient over the Sahel, but a reduction in the total number of rainy days.

How variability of Sahel rainfall on interannual timescales will change in a warmer and wetter mean climate under greenhouse warming is unclear. Using the latest climate models in CMIP6, here we show a robust increase in JAS Sahel rainfall variability in the 21st century under a high emission scenario, accompanied by an increase in both extreme dry and wet seasons.
